div.p: For a number of years, work has been performed in collaboration with industry to establish improved techniques for achieving and proving the system timing constraints. The specijic requirements encountered during the course of this work for both uniprocessor and distributed systems indicate a need for an eficient mechanism for handling the timing analysis of task sets which feature offsets. Little research has been performed on this subject. This paper will describe a new technique tailored to a set of real world problems so that the results are effective and the complexity is manageable.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: The majority of the timing analysis performed to date has assumed a critical instant. Liu and Layland [4] state that for tasks sets which feature no offsets there is a critical instant where all tasks are simultaneously released. If the timing analysis is carried out for the critical instant and we assume all tasks execute for their worst case time, then tests exists that are both sufficient and necessary. However, in practical systems it is frequently necessary to offset the execution of tasks from one another. In these cases, the test based on a critical instant becomes pessimistic. Offsets are used within real systems so that actual requirements and design derived requirements can be met. There are a number of reasons why we would wish to use offsets in a system, including:

1. Actual Requirement: Ensuring a particular action has been performed before releasing another task. For example, task A may request data from a hardware device, however, the data may not be available for a time X milli-seconds later. Therefore, an associated task B is required to read the data and be offset by an appropriate amount. 0-8186-8034-2197 $10.00 0 1997 IEEE

div.head: Design Derived Requirement (A):
div.p: The spreading of processor resource requirements through a given time frame so that jitter is reduced.

div.head: Design Derived Requirement (B):
div.p: Ensuring precedence relations are maintained by not allowing a task to be released until another has completed its execution.

A useful observation is that all of these requirements are flexible in nature. For example, with the first item in the previous list as long as a minimum separation between the two tasks is maintained, and the second task meets its required deadline, then the actual offset does not matter. The approach taken within this paper will utilise the flexibility available.

A number of approaches [l, 51 have been attempted to extend the standard timing analysis to cater for task sets with offsets. Section 2 of this paper will provide background information on the timing analysis used when the task set does not feature offsets. This paper will then discuss three approaches to the timing analysis of offsets. Section 3 will discuss the existing pessimistic approach where task offsets are ignored and it is assumed there is a critical instance. Section 4 discusses the exact analysis approach, where each individual task release is checked for schedulability for the minimum period that the execution order does not repeat. Section 5 has the new approach which entails forming a composite task with no offset to represent the tasks with offsets. Section 6 will present an improved blocking model for use in the timing analysis in general, its effectiveness demonstrated with the new offset analysis approach. Finally, section 7 of the paper presents some conclusions.

div.head: Timing Analysis
div.p: This section will present the conventional timing analysis for uniprocessor systems. The scheduling model which the analysis is based upon is a non-preemptive scheduler where tasks have unique priorities, zero offsets, and deadlines less than or equal to the period. div.p: Simple analysis of task sets with offsets can be carried out by effectively ignoring the offsets and assuming a critical instant, i.e. the simultaneous release of all tasks. div.head: Exact Analysis
div.p: The exact form of analysis takes the approach of showing every individual release of a task is schedulable assuming all tasks execute for their worst case execution time. The original consideration of offsets was performed by Leung [3] which shows that if every invocation of every task is schedulable over the period [max (Oi). 2xLeast Common Multiple (Ti) + max (0;)) then the task set is schedulable.
Later Audsley [ 11 improved the analysis so the duration became [max (Oi), Least Common Multiple (Ti) + max (Oi)).

The exact analysis approach does not suffer the pessimism of other approaches which largely comes from two areas. Firstly, task sets with offsets do not have a critical instant. Therefore, the resource is effectively spread through time and all tasks are not simultaneously released. This will lead to a lower value for the worst case response time.

Secondly. the blocking model' for timing analysis based on the critical instant introduces pessimism, since it is assumed every task can block each other. This is clearly pessimistic because it relies on the assumption that the task being analysed is runnable when any of the lower priority task is being run. There are many cases where this will not be true.

The problem with the exact analysis approach is that for task sets which feature co-prime periods then the number of releases that require checking may become prohibitively large. Table 3 illustrates the number of releases for the example task set in Table 1. Using the exact analysis approach it is possible to show that the task set is schedulable as shown in Table 4. But, if 2 tasks are added to the task set with iteration rates of 97000 and 37000 then the number of releases becomes 97 x 37x 196 = 703444. This number is quickly becoming large and when it is considered the task sets typically contain upwards of 70 tasks then the computational complexity may result in an effectively infeasible problem.

div.head: A Composite Approach
div.p: Our experience in performing timing analysis of real industrial systems lead us to the observation that there was a particular pattern to the types of offset used. Firstly, as the introduction outlined the specified values were relatively flexible. Secondly, their use was analoguous to that of the cyclic executive, i.e. the processing frame was split into manageable chunks with tasks allocated to the different partitions using offsets. Table 1 illustrates the type of requirement that results. In Table 1, tasks A, B, C , D have offsets such that their computation is spaced over the period of 25000 units. This section will present an approach based on the formation of composite tasks that are used for analysis purposes only, i.e. the composite task does not feature as part of the implementation. The motivation behind this approach is that if a composite task with zero offset can represent the tasks with non-zero offsets then the analysis presented in equation ( 1) may be used. The benefit of the composite task approach is that computational complexity is kept sufficiently low, while allowing the resource to be spread through time. div.head: Proof of Correctness
div.p: Obviously, with any new approach to timing analysis it is important to show that it is a sufficient test. A sufficient test is where if the test indicates that the system meets the requirement, then in practice it will. However, if the results suggest the system does not meet the requirement then in practice the system may still do so. In this respect the test can be referred to as pessimistic. Tindell [5] showed a test is sufficient when the interference experienced by all lower priority tasks does not decrease compared to another sufficient test.
Theorem 1 Show that the interference experienced by all lower priority tasks does not decrease compared to another sufficient test.

div.head: Selection of Offsets
div.p: The rigorous treatment of offsets is a new area which allows the developer scope to optimise the chosen timing constraints. At present, it is known that there is a need for offsets within the system, however there is no definition to date of what they should be. Therefore, it is proposed that to some extent we treat the offset and deadline as a relatively "free variable". The aim would be to choose the values of offsets to enforce the necessary requirement as well as to optimise the schedulability analysis.

The approach that could be taken is to split the offset tasks up in a similar fashion to allocating tasks in the cyclic executive schedule. This approach could result in tasks having greater offsets than necessary, however this could provide better results. In the event that the offset values provided are not great enough to map the system requirements to tasks then in effect the number of slots could be increased, i.e. a choice of 0, 6 , g, .., v, where M is greater than N.

If the task set in Table 1 is considered using the free variable argument with M=N, this would result in the tasks A, B, C , D having offsets of 0,6250, 12500 and 18750 respectively. This would be invalid since task C's offset would be decreased. However, if M=5 then the offsets of tasks A, B, C , D would be 0, 5000, 15000 and 20000 respectively. It should be noted that in this case the value of TCOMP would be worse. The reason is the flexibility in requirements has not been utilised, i.e. task C's offset could probably be 12500 without affecting the system operation.

'If tasks with a lower priority than the set of tasks ST did receive higher priorities then the worst case response time would again increase, since the interference term for a task is always greater than the blocking term.

In many cases, the task deadlines may also be treated in a similar manner as the offsets. Consideration of equation ( 10) shows the deadlines are maximised if they are equivalent to the offset of the following task. Therefore, wherever possible this approach shall be used.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: Within this paper new timing analysis for task sets featuring offsets has been described. The approach is based on altering the task set characteristics for analysis purposes only, so that it is more amenable to analysis. The analysis 4The shaded boxes represent the Worst Case Response Time (WCRT) of a particular task release. has shown the approach is effective for the systems commonly encountered by practitioners whilst being computationally feasible. Also, an improved blocking model has been formed which is deemed to be particularly appropriate for task sets with largely harmonic periods.

The intention is to use the two forms of analysis within an being developed for distributed systems. The aim is to utilise the free variable argument wherever possible to improve the effectiveness of the analysis. The distributed systems work is intended for use on the next generation of aircraft engine controllers currently being developed.
